title: Floods and a Quake Couldn't Break This 1,400-Year-Old Chinese Bridge | China Travel Expert
description:
China's Zhaozhou Bridge (赵州桥, also called Anji Bridge) was built around 605 CE during the Sui dynasty — making it roughly 1,400 years old and the world's oldest surviving open-spandrel segmental stone arch bridge. It is still standing, and still walkable.

Here is the engineering trick you can see in the animation: instead of a tall half-circle, its designer Li Chun used one shallow arch about 37 m across but only about 7 m high — and then opened four small arches in the shoulders instead of packing them with solid stone. Those openings cut the stone's weight by roughly 15–20%, and in a flood they let water pour straight through the bridge instead of slamming into a solid wall. China Daily reports the open design increased the water-flow area by about 16.5%. That is a big reason the bridge has outlasted floods and earthquakes — including the magnitude-7.2 Xingtai quake in 1966 — with its load-bearing structure intact.

Expert Tip: the next time you see an old stone arch bridge, look at the shoulders. Little arches sitting on the big one means an 'open-spandrel' design — lighter, and built to survive floods.

赵州桥建于约公元605年（隋朝），距今约1400年，是世界上现存最古老的敞肩石拱桥。设计师李春用一个又宽又扁的大拱（跨约37米、高仅约7米），再在两肩各开两个小拱，既减轻自重约15–20%，发大水时又能让洪水从小拱穿过。一千四百年、无数次洪水和一场7.2级地震都没把它压垮。老石头和新钢材，你更信哪一个？
